summary: Defines SNMP management objects for IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, covering 10 and 100 Mb/s Ethernet. Network managers can use it to inspect and configure those interfaces. It was replaced by RFC 2668.

eli5.summary: It gives managers a standard way to check the wired connection on an Ethernet device and see how fast it is running.

subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and controlling the transceivers that attach 10 and 100 Mb/s Ethernet devices to the wire.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to inspect and control the Medium Attachment Units (MAUs) that connect IEEE 802.3 repeaters and interfaces to their media, including the new 100 Mb/s types.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2239 defines an SNMPv2 MIB module, MAU-MIB, with tables for repeater MAUs, interface MAUs, jacks, auto-negotiation and broadband MAUs, plus two jabber notifications. It is a superset of the earlier RFC 1515 MIB.
tldr.outcome: It has been obsoleted by RFC 2668, so that document is the one to use for the MAU MIB.

today: RFC 2239 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2668, which should be used for the MAU MIB instead.

sections.title: What the MAU MIB Covers
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing 10 and 100 Mb/second Medium Attachment Units (MAUs), based on IEEE Std 802.3 Section 30, "10 & 100 Mb/s Management". Instances of the objects represent attributes of an IEEE 802.3 MAU. For convenience the RFC calls MAUs connected to 802.3 repeaters "repeater MAUs" and those connected to Ethernet-like interfaces "interface MAUs".

The MIB is intended to be a superset of the one in RFC 1515, which the RFC says will go to historic status. It keeps all the old objects and adds management of 100 Mb/s devices, auto-negotiation on interface MAUs and jack management. Implementors are encouraged to support all applicable conformance groups.
sections.eli5: A MAU is the part that plugs a device into the wire. This RFC lists the things a manager is allowed to ask about it, for both older and faster wiring.

sections.title: How It Fits With Other MIBs
sections.content:
An agent implementing this MIB is assumed to implement at least the system group of MIB-II. The interface-MAU objects extend the MIB-II interfaces group, so an agent that implements them must also implement that group. The value of ifMauIfIndex is the same as the ifIndex of the interface the MAU is connected to. The RFC expects such an agent to also implement the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB, RFC 1650.

The repeater-MAU objects extend the 802.3 Repeater MIB, which the agent must also implement. Repeater ports are not interfaces in the MIB-II sense, so the group and port indexes of a repeater MAU match those of the port it is connected to.

A MAU can be "internal", with its functionality implemented entirely inside a device. Internal MAUs may or may not be managed. If they are, their objects appear under dot3RpMauBasicGroup for repeater MAUs and dot3IfMauBasicGroup for interface MAUs.
sections.eli5: The MAU list is an add-on to lists that already exist, so it uses the same numbering for ports and interfaces to say which one a MAU belongs to.

sections.title: Tables and Objects
sections.content:
The module is rooted at snmpDot3MauMgt, which is { mib-2 26 }. A set of object identities names the MAU types, from dot3MauTypeAUI and dot3MauType10Base5 up to dot3MauType100BaseT2FD. The ones new since RFC 1515 cover the duplex variants and the 100 Mb/s types. A JackType textual convention lists connectors such as rj45, bnc and fiberSC.

  • rpMauTable describes repeater MAUs, indexed by group, port and MAU. It has the type, status, media availability, jabber state and counters such as rpMauFalseCarriers.
  • ifMauTable describes interface MAUs with similar objects, plus ifMauTypeList, ifMauDefaultType and ifMauAutoNegSupported.
  • rpJackTable and ifJackTable give the connector type on the outside of the system.
  • broadMauBasicTable covers 10BROAD36 broadband MAUs, with split type and carrier frequencies in units of 250 kHz.

The status object can be read or written. Values include operational, standby, shutdown and reset, and the RFC says an agent may implement it read-only if it has no software control of the MAU. The media-available object reports states such as available, notAvailable and remoteFault.
sections.eli5: There are tables, like spreadsheets, with one row per connector part. Columns say what kind of connector it is, whether the link is up and how often something went wrong.

sections.title: Auto-Negotiation Objects
sections.content:
The ifMauAutoNegTable applies to systems where auto-negotiation is supported on interface MAUs. When auto-negotiation is present and enabled, ifMauType reflects its result. Otherwise the operational type is set by ifMauDefaultType, and writing that object forces the MAU into the new mode.

Setting ifMauAutoNegAdminStatus to enabled turns on auto-negotiation signaling. Setting it to disabled forces the MAU to the type in ifMauDefaultType, and agents must make the reported type follow. Other objects show whether the remote end uses auto-negotiation signaling, the state of the process (including parallelDetectFail), the local capabilities, the capabilities advertised and those received. Writing restart to ifMauAutoNegRestart forces renegotiation.

Capabilities are bit sums. Each capability adds 2 raised to a listed power, so a MAU that can only do 10BASE-T has the value 512 (2**9) in ifMauTypeList.
sections.eli5: Auto-negotiation is two devices agreeing on the best speed they both can do. These objects let a manager see what each side offered and tell them to try again.

sections.title: Jabber Notifications
sections.content:
A MAU that transmits without stopping is said to be jabbering. The module defines two notifications, rpMauJabberTrap for repeater MAUs and ifMauJabberTrap for interface MAUs, sent whenever a managed MAU enters the jabber state. The agent must throttle consecutive traps so that there is at least a five-second gap between them.

Conformance is organized in groups. The basic repeater and interface groups are mandatory for their compliance statements, the 100 Mb/s and jack groups are recommended where they apply, and the auto-negotiation and broadband groups are mandatory for MAUs that support those features.
sections.eli5: If a connector part gets stuck shouting, it can send an alarm to the manager. It may only ring the alarm once every five seconds, so it does not flood the line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some of the information in this MIB may be sensitive, so authentication of SNMP requests and controlled access to management information should be used in such environments. The method is a function of the SNMP Administrative Framework and is not expanded by this MIB.

Several objects allow write access. Setting them can seriously affect the network, including enabling or disabling a MAU, changing its default type, enabling, disabling or restarting auto-negotiation, or changing the capabilities it advertises. Implementers are urged to consider whether set operations should be allowed without at least authenticating the request origin.
sections.eli5: Some of these controls can switch a network connection off. So only people who can prove who they are should be allowed to use them.
